title: Caste in your own life
hook: noticing caste thinking in yourself and your family
tomorrow: Sunday lunch: the women cook, the men sit. does Simran say it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, acceptance and rising: bhaana and chardi kala in one breath, and the Ardas asking for the good of all. All is a big word. Today tests it at the dinner table.
screen: `ACCEPT, THEN RISE.` → `THE GOOD OF ALL, AT DINNER.`

segments.voice: Some questions sound like small talk and aren't. So, what does your family do? Which part of town? What's your last name again? At dinner, Simran is telling the bus stop story, proud of Arjan for holding his head up, and Bebe asks, mildly, what his family's surname is. Simran answers. Bebe nods, the way people nod when they've placed someone. Nobody says the word caste. Nobody has to. Simran puts her fork down. So the question on the table is old: does the family you're born into rank you?
screen: `WHAT'S YOUR LAST NAME AGAIN?` → `BEBE NODS, AND PLACES HIM.` → `NOBODY SAYS THE WORD.` → `DOES BIRTH RANK YOU?`

segments.voice: The Gurus answer no, plainly. Guru Nanak says on Ang 349, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; hereafter, there is no caste. Guru Gobind Singh, in the Akal Ustat, puts it in one line: manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo, recognize the whole human race as one. That's the line to tell a friend tonight: one human caste, in a Guru's own words. And the langar puts it in your knees: everyone sits in one row, the pangat, and eats the same food. Honesty matters here too. Caste names still linger in some Sikh families, in surnames, in marriage talk, in a nod at dinner. That's why today is about your own life, not someone else's. A neighbor tradition says something close. Paul, standing in Athens in the Book of Acts, tells the crowd that God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.” Shared ground: one human family, no ranking by birth. And one honest difference. Paul grounds it in one blood, a common origin from one Maker. Guru Nanak grounds it in one light, shining now inside each person. Simran asks Bebe, quietly, why the name mattered. Bebe is quiet for a long time. Then: it mattered in my village. Let me think about your kitchen.
screen: `SEE THE LIGHT, DON'T ASK THE CASTE.` · `THE WHOLE HUMAN RACE AS ONE.` · `ACTS: OF ONE BLOOD ALL NATIONS.` · `ONE BLOOD, ONE LIGHT.` · then, large: `NO CASTE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write down one quick judgment you've caught yourself making about someone because of their family, their name, or where they're from. Under it, write: recognize the light. Read both lines slowly, and leave the paper where you'll see it.
Caste in your own life. Noticing the quiet ranking by birth in yourself and your family, and choosing the light over the name.
screen: `CASTE IN YOUR OWN LIFE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Carry this: no caste, one light, one human race. Bebe is still thinking, and that counts for day 1728.

screen: `DAY 1728 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 102 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: THE WOMEN COOK, THE MEN SIT. DOES SIMRAN SAY IT?`
